headline: Nyatt Point on the push: bass working structure as the moon crowds full
subhead: Fluke are spreading thin in the warm water, but the tide swings building into Friday's full moon are about to sharpen every bite window in the bay.
body_markdown:
Down at the Providence River piers this week the talk wasn't about big fish, it was about timing. Guys standing around the bait shop counter with a scoop of green crabs in one hand were all saying the same thing — the bass are here, but they're not dumb, and if you're not fishing the turn of the tide you're just casting at empty water. That's late August on this bay. The water's warm on the surface, the bait's shifted from the herring that ran up Buckeye Brook back in April to silversides and peanut menhaden working the flats and the edges of Greenwich Bay, and the fish know exactly when the tide is going to stack that bait against a rock pile or a bridge piling. Miss the window and you're watching gulls instead of hooking up.

The moon is closing in on full tomorrow night, and that's the story for the next several days. Bigger tidal swings mean more water moving through the East and West Passages, which means the current seams off Nyatt Point, Rocky Point, and the north end of Prudence Island are going to load up harder and longer than they have the past couple weeks. We flagged this pattern building last week — said the push toward full moon would strengthen the current that pins bait against structure, and that's exactly what's setting up now. The guys working Rocky Point after dark have been getting into slot bass on the last two hours of the incoming, throwing bunker chunks and swimming plugs tight to the ledge rock, and that bite should only get better as the tide range opens up into the weekend.

Striped bass overall are in that predictable late-summer holding pattern — nobody's expecting a blitz with the surface water sitting where it is, but the structure bite is real if you fish it on the tide change instead of the middle of the day. Nyatt Point's rock pile has been giving up fish on the last of the ebb into the start of the flood, mostly schoolies to mid-20s with the occasional better fish mixed in, taken on white bucktails tipped with a swimming mullet or live eels drifted along the drop. Conimicut Point is still holding fish too, especially right at first light before the boat traffic picks up — that flat drops off fast on the east side and bass will sit right on that break waiting for bait to get pushed off the flat on the outgoing.

Fluke are the tougher story right now, and there's no sense pretending otherwise. The warm surface layer has spread them out across the flats instead of concentrating them, so the easy days of drifting anywhere in Greenwich Bay and connecting are over for the moment. The better fish are coming off channel edges and deeper water where there's still a cooler bottom layer holding — the mouth of Greenwich Bay where it drops into the main channel, and the deeper water off the west side of Prudence Island, have both been producing keeper-class fluke in the 18 to 22 inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right on bottom through the last two hours of the outgoing. Anybody fishing the shallow flats in the middle of the day is mostly finding shorts.

Bluefish are doing what bluefish do — filling in the gaps. Snapper blues are thick in the coves around Greenwich Bay and up in the quieter corners off Rocky Point, plenty of fun for kids off the dock on small Kastmasters or a strip of squid under a bobber. The bigger cocktail blues, a pound and a half to three pounds, are mixing right in with the striper catches on structure, so if you're bucktailing for bass off Nyatt Point don't be surprised when a blue cuts your leader instead.

Scup fishing has been steady on the rocky ledges, which is about as reliable as this bay gets in August. Rocky Point and the rock piles off Nyatt are stacked with them, especially on the slower parts of the tide when the current isn't ripping too hard to hold bottom. Sandworms and clam on a simple hi-lo rig, 12 to 20 feet of water, will fill a bucket without much drama. Black sea bass are showing as a bonus catch on the same deeper structure around Prudence Island, nothing to build a trip around but a welcome addition when they show up on the same bait.

The one thing generating real chatter down at the docks is bonito. Nothing confirmed inside the bay yet, but there's scouting talk filtering up from the lower bay and the breachways toward Newport — guys seeing bait get nervous and boils that don't look like bluefish. Worth keeping an eye on the East Passage mouth and the water off the south end of Prudence over the next week if that pattern firms up.

Looking ahead, the full moon tomorrow night should be the pivot point. Expect the tidal swings to keep building through the weekend, which will sharpen the structure bite on bass at Nyatt Point and Rocky Point and should push more bait through the channel edges where the fluke have been holding. If you can only fish one tide this week, make it the two hours around the top of the flood at Rocky Point after dark — that's where the current and the structure are lining up best right now.
